claims.text: Controlled heat treatment can adjust grain size, grain-boundary density, and precipitate distribution while keeping bulk alloy chemistry constant.
Optimizing the steel microstructure enhances formation of a chromium-enriched passive film.
Optimizing the steel microstructure enhances the self-healing ability of the chromium-enriched passive film.
Enhanced formation and self-healing of the chromium-enriched passive film improve corrosion resistance under simulated chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions.
Increased grain-boundary density enhances the kinetics and stability of passive-film formation.
Optimized precipitate distributions enhance the kinetics and stability of passive-film formation.
Increased grain-boundary density and optimized precipitate distributions promote rapid repair of passive-film defects under aggressive conditions.
Microstructure-optimized steel will have a more stable passive film than the untreated baseline.
Microstructure-optimized steel will exhibit lower corrosion current density than the untreated baseline.
Microstructure-optimized steel will exhibit a more noble corrosion potential than the untreated baseline.
Surface analysis will show better passive-film integrity on microstructure-optimized steel than on the untreated baseline.
The proposed mechanism should apply to steels of similar alloy composition within the tested pH, temperature, and radiation-dose ranges.
The heat-treated and as-received groups will be exposed to identical chemical and simulated irradiation conditions.
Corrosion current density, corrosion potential, passive-film composition and integrity, and microstructural features will be measured.
The hypothesis will be falsified if treated samples show no statistically significant passivation improvement relative to untreated controls under identical conditions.
